content: Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW) is an isotopic water standard established in 1968 by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Despite its name, which might suggest a connection to seawater, VSMOW refers to pure water (H₂O) without any salts or other substances typically found in ocean water. It is primarily used as a reference standard for comparing the ratios of hydrogen and oxygen isotopes in water samples. However, these were refined in the 1960s with the development of the Standard Mean Ocean Water (SMOW) definition. The U.S. National Bureau of Standards (now known as the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST) initially created physical water standards for global use, but concerns arose regarding their physical integrity. In response, VSMOW was developed in 1967 by Harmon Craig and colleagues at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography. They created VSMOW by mixing distilled ocean waters collected from various locations worldwide. Today, VSMOW remains a critical isotopic water benchmark. The isotopic composition of VSMOW is defined by the molar abundance ratios of rare isotopes to their most common counterparts, expressed in parts per million (ppm). For example: The ratio of deuterium (²H) to protium (¹H) is 155.76 ± 0.1 ppm, meaning there is approximately one deuterium atom for every 6,420 hydrogen atoms. The ratio of tritium (³H) to protium (¹H) is 1.85 ± 0. The ratio of oxygen-18 (¹⁸O) to oxygen-16 (¹⁶O) is 2005.20 ± 0.43 ppm, or about one ¹⁸O atom for every 498.7 oxygen atoms. The ratio of oxygen-17 (¹⁷O) to oxygen-16 (¹⁶O) is 379.9 ± 1.6 ppm, or about one ¹⁷O atom for every 2,632 oxygen atoms. Both the Kelvin and Celsius temperature scales are defined using the triple point of water, which is 273.16 K (0.01 °C). For this reason, VSMOW is used as the standard water for defining the triple point. Water molecules containing different isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen evaporate at varying rates and temperatures, leading to isotopic enrichment in lighter isotopes in natural water sources like snow, rivers, and rain. Triple-point temperature reference cells filled with water of incorrect isotopic composition can introduce errors of several hundred microkelvins (µK).01 °C and 273.16 K.325 kPa) are no longer used as defining points for the Celsius scale.000089(10) °C, and the boiling point is 99. When calibrated to the International Temperature Scale of 1990 (ITS-90), the boiling point is slightly lower, at approximately 99.974 °C. For instance, a change in altitude of just 28 cm (11 inches) can alter the boiling point by one millikelvin. The physical properties of VSMOW are as follows: Maximum liquid density: 999.97495 kg/m³ at 3.984 °C. Density of melting ice: 916.8 kg/m³. Melting point: +0.000089(10) °C. Triple point: 0.01 °C (exactly, by definition) at 611.657 Pa. Boiling point at 101.325 kPa: 99.9839 °C (or 99.974 °C when calibrated to ITS-90). Molar mass: 18.015268 grams per mole.
